To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) coping with CHD-specific stress is related to better emotional functioning and (2) involuntary stress reactivity moderates the association between primary and secondary control coping and emotional distress.

Secondary control coping (e..g. cognitive restructuring, positive reframing, acceptance) is associated with lower depression and anxiety, whereas primary control coping (e. g., problem solving) is associated with higher depression and anxiety.

(a) secondary control coping (i.e., cognitive restructuring) predicted lower depression, and (b), the association between primary coping and lower depression was stronger among individuals with higher levels of involuntary stress reactivity (i.e., rumination, numbing).
